ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: The Department of Medical Microbiology studies microorganisms that cause disease, their detection, and control. Clinicians use microbiology to diagnose infections, guide therapy, and prevent outbreaks. In low‑resource settings, rapid, affordable tests and infection control are key.

sections.p: Microbiology examines bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites that infect humans. Clinicians rely on lab results to identify pathogens, determine resistance, and choose treatment. The department also develops infection control policies.
b: Focus on identification, susceptibility, and prevention

sections.p: Microorganisms are classified by shape, Gram stain, oxygen requirement, and metabolic traits. These features guide initial lab tests and empirical therapy.
Infections spread via droplets, contact, vectors, or food. Understanding routes informs isolation, vaccination, and vector control.
Microbes cause a spectrum from mild infections to sepsis. Severity depends on host immunity, pathogen virulence, and delay in treatment.
Diagnosis combines clinical clues with targeted tests. In low‑resource settings, point‑of‑care tests and simple cultures are vital.

sections.p: Treat the identified pathogen with appropriate antimicrobials, while providing supportive care. Infection control prevents spread.

t.b: Select based on organism and resistance pattern; avoid nephrotoxic drugs in renal failure.
Maintain fluids, oxygen, and monitor organ function.

sections.p: Remember that culture growth time varies; Gram stain gives early clues. In low‑resource settings, use clinical scoring (e.g., qSOFA) to triage sepsis.
b: Empirical antibiotics for sepsis should cover MRSA and gram‑negatives

sections.p: Some infections mimic each other; clinical context and simple tests help differentiate.
Low bacterial load may give false‑negative cultures; malaria RDTs may miss low parasitemia.
Urgent care needed for severe sepsis, meningitis, or suspected drug allergy.

faq.q: What is the first step in managing suspected sepsis?
faq.a: Obtain blood cultures, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and give fluids.

faq.q: How do I differentiate bacterial from viral pneumonia?
faq.a: Look for high fever, productive cough, and positive Gram stain; viral often has dry cough and rapid onset.

faq.q: When can I rely on a rapid malaria test?
faq.a: Use it when fever is present and microscopy is unavailable; confirm with microscopy if possible.

exam: Explain how a Gram stain guides empirical antibiotic choice in a patient with suspected bacterial sepsis.
Describe the steps to diagnose and treat a patient with suspected malaria in a rural clinic.
Outline infection control measures to prevent MRSA spread in a low‑resource hospital.
